summary: Specifies the Internet Control Message Protocol messages for use with IPv6, which carry error and diagnostic information between hosts and routers. It was standards-track and was replaced by RFC 2463.

plainLanguage.summary: The messenger that tells you when a packet couldn't be delivered, or that checks whether a machine is there.

questions: how does icmpv6 error reporting work
subtitle: The control messages IPv6 uses to report errors and perform diagnostics.

tldr.problem: IPv6 nodes need a way to report problems when packets cannot be delivered or processed, and to perform network diagnostics like checking if a host is reachable.
tldr.mechanism: ICMPv6 defines control messages for error reporting (destination unreachable, packet too big, time exceeded, parameter problem) and informational queries (echo request/reply, group membership messages).
tldr.outcome: RFC 1885 was replaced by RFC 2463, which is the current standard. ICMPv6 is mandatory in all IPv6 implementations and essential for network operation.

today: RFC 1885 was obsoleted by RFC 2463, which clarified certain edge cases and processing rules. However, RFC 2463 has itself been updated, and the current standard for ICMPv6 is RFC 4443. ICMPv6 remains mandatory in all IPv6 implementations and is essential for network diagnostics, error reporting, and multicast group management.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ICMPv6 (Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6) is a fundamental part of every IPv6 implementation. It carries error messages and diagnostic information between IPv6 hosts and routers. RFC 1885 merges ICMP functionality from IPv4 with the IPv6 Group Membership Protocol, creating a single, unified control mechanism for IPv6 networks.

Unlike IPv4, where ICMP and multicast group management are separate protocols, ICMPv6 combines these functions. It is identified by the Next Header value of 58 in IPv6 packets.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMPv6 is the messenger that delivers bad news on an IPv6 network. When something goes wrong or needs checking, ICMPv6 carries the message back to whoever sent the packet that caused the problem.

sections.title: Message Format and Types
sections.content:
All ICMPv6 messages share a common structure with a Type field, Code field, and Checksum. The Type field determines the message category: error messages have types 0 to 127, while informational messages have types 128 to 255.

The RFC defines four error messages: Destination Unreachable (type 1), Packet Too Big (type 2), Time Exceeded (type 3), and Parameter Problem (type 4). It also defines three informational messages: Echo Request (type 128), Echo Reply (type 129), and Group Membership Messages (types 130, 131, 132). Each type has a Code field that provides additional specificity about the condition.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of ICMPv6 messages like different kinds of error notes. The Type tells you the main problem (packet too big, destination unreachable, etc.), and the Code gives more details (like which specific reason).

sections.title: Error Messages
sections.content:
Error messages are sent in response to packets that cannot be processed. The Destination Unreachable message (type 1) indicates a packet cannot reach its target due to five possible reasons: no route to destination, administrative prohibition (firewall), not a neighbor (routing header violation), address unreachable, or port unreachable.

The Packet Too Big message (type 2) signals that a router cannot forward a packet because it exceeds the MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) of the outgoing link. This message is critical for Path MTU Discovery. The Time Exceeded message (type 3) is sent when a packet's Hop Limit reaches zero, indicating a routing loop or insufficient initial Hop Limit value.

The Parameter Problem message (type 4) reports errors in the IPv6 header or extension headers. A Pointer field identifies the exact octet in the offending packet where the error was detected. Error messages include as much of the original packet as possible (up to 576 octets) to help upper-layer protocols process the error.
sections.plainLanguage: Error messages are like different kinds of rejection slips. One says 'we can't find that address', another says 'the message is too big for our link', another says 'the packet bounced around too many times'. Each one includes a copy of the message that caused the problem so the sender can figure out what went wrong.

sections.title: Informational Messages
sections.content:
ICMPv6 Echo Request and Echo Reply messages enable the ping diagnostic tool. An Echo Request (type 128) contains an Identifier and Sequence Number to match replies, plus optional data. The receiver must respond with an Echo Reply (type 129) containing the same Identifier, Sequence Number, and data. Echo Replies must be sent to the source address of the request.

Group Membership Messages (types 130, 131, 132) inherited from IPv4's IGMP handle IPv6 multicast group management. A Group Membership Query (type 130) asks which nodes are members of a multicast group. Nodes respond with a Group Membership Report (type 131) to indicate membership. A Group Membership Reduction (type 132) signals when a node leaves a multicast group.
sections.plainLanguage: Informational messages are mostly about asking 'are you there?' and managing club memberships. Echo asks 'are you listening?' and the other node echoes back to say yes. Group Membership messages are like raising your hand to join or leave a group chat.

sections.title: Processing and Rate Limiting
sections.content:
ICMPv6 implementations must follow strict processing rules to prevent abuse and network loops. Error messages MUST NOT be sent in response to other error messages; this prevents cascading failure scenarios. An exception allows Packet Too Big messages and certain Parameter Problem messages to be sent even in response to multicast or link-layer broadcast packets, because Path MTU Discovery requires this.

Implementations MUST limit the rate at which ICMPv6 error messages are sent to any single source. Rate limiting can be timer-based (e.g., at most one message per second) or bandwidth-based (e.g., at most 2 percent of link bandwidth). Conservative default values are required. Error messages must also include sufficient context from the offending packet for upper-layer protocols to process them, but packets larger than 576 octets are truncated.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules prevent ICMPv6 from becoming a spam machine. You don't send error messages in response to error messages (that would create an infinite loop), and you limit how many error messages you send to someone who keeps messing up. It's like saying 'I'll only complain once a second, not a million times.'

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type (0-127 for errors, 128-255 for informational).

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Additional message specificity, depends on Type field.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Checksum computed over ICMPv6 message and IPv6 pseudo-header.
